title: Autoscaler config drift detection & nightshift remediation log
content:
Context:
This is a raw nightshift log capturing detection of an autoscaler config drift that caused gradual GPU pool degradation for Dedicated customers. Goal: capture quick hypotheses, immediate mitigations, and a lightweight follow-up checklist so the day team can triage without starting from zero.

Summary timeline (high level):
- 2024-11-07 02:10 UTC: Pager triggered for dedicated-pool-7 latency increase (p50->p95 spike). Signal: per-tenant tail latency and rejected-requests.
- 02:13: initial Slack thread #sre-dedicated created by oncall (Jordan).
- 02:20: Found recent automated config push to autoscaler pool (ops-configs PR merged 2024-11-06 23:45). Suspect hysteresis/growth-rate tweak.
- 02:30: Scaled pool up manually (add 4 nodes) as emergency mitigation — reduced p95 by ~25%.
- 02:45: Continue to observe intermittent KV-cache thrash; hypothesis expanded to prefix-cache eviction interaction with larger scale events.
- 03:10: Reverted autoscaler config to previous commit (rollback PR) — metrics stabilized within 30m.
- 03:55: Post-incident notes captured; transfer to daytime owners.

Immediate observations (notes to self):
- Pager was noisy but valid — multiple tenants saw latency regressions and request rejections at the same time as autoscaler actions.
- The merged config change shortened cooldown/hysteresis and increased growth_factor from 1.2->1.6. That made the autoscaler more aggressive in scale-ups but also increased oscillation risk when paired with our burst-smoothing policy.
- Our monitor alerts are based on aggregated signals; we want a per-pool hysteresis-safety-signal to avoid cascade scaling on transient request bursts from a noisy tenant.
- KV-cache eviction (prefix cache) shows increased churn when new nodes come in/out quickly. This increased token-serving latency for warm sessions.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Config drift: new autoscaler parameters reduced hysteresis so the controller repeatedly scales pool up/down in response to noisy short-lived throughput bursts. Rapid scale events cause KV cache warming penalties and upstream request rejections while nodes join/leave.
2) Noisy tenant amplification: one tenant generated a high short-burst load (detected in tenant-id=tn-994) causing autoscaler to overreact; anti-noise protections are insufficient.
3) Orchestration timing bug: scale-up triggered before scheduler fully prepared instances; LB healthchecks reported ready earlier than application-level readiness, causing a temporary pool of insufficiently warmed workers.

Evidence collected (quick links & queries run):
- Cloud metrics: query cpu_utilization, token_latency_p95, rejected_requests_by_tenant for pool=dedicated-pool-7, time window 02:00-04:00 UTC.
- Autoscaler audit log: ops-configs commit 4f3a2b (merged 2024-11-06 23:45), change set includes hysteresis=30s->10s, growth_factor=1.2->1.6.
- Kubernetes events: rapid ReplicaSet creation/deletion spikes correlating with autoscaler commands at 02:12, 02:18, 02:24.
- KV cache eviction rate: 02:10->03:00 eviction_rate x3 baseline.
- Tenant activity: tn-994 had 6x normal request bursts between 02:05-02:25, mostly short-lived.

Actions taken (chronological, with commands we ran):
- 02:22: emergency scale: aws/gcloud cli add nodes +4 to dedicated-pool-7 (manual override). Result: p95 reduced but oscillations remained.
- 02:35: Isolated tn-994 traffic by rate-limiting at ingress (temporary rule in edge-router). Immediate reduction in rejected_requests for other tenants.
- 02:50: Rolling revert: applied rollback of autoscaler params to commit 9b8c1e (previous stable).
  Commands: git revert 4f3a2b && terraform apply -target=module.autoscaler.pool7
- 03:05: Monitored KV cache steady-state — eviction rate decreased and latency returned to baseline by ~03:35.

What worked:
- Manual scale-up bought time to avoid immediate customer impact while we evaluated root cause.
- Quick rollback of autoscaler params was effective in stopping the oscillation and letting caches stabilize.
- Tenant isolation via temporary ingress rule prevented cross-tenant blowup and gave us a cleaner signal to validate the rollback.

What didn't work / rough edges:
- Our autoscaler rollout lacked a gated canary for aggressive parameter changes; small parameter changes were allowed straight to prod.
- Monitoring thresholds were too coarse; the alert fired but didn't immediately identify config change as likely cause. We should route config-change triggers to a 'config' alert channel.
- No fast verification harness existed to simulate warm KV-cache impact for a rolling scale event. We have synthetic tests for throughput but not for cache-warming latency.

Short follow-up checklist (for daytime owners):
- [ ] Create a gated rollout pattern for autoscaler parameter changes: require canary pool with identical workload for 30m. (Owner: Priya)
- [ ] Add a config-change correlation alert that flags recent ops-configs merges when a pool latency alert fires. (Owner: Luca)
- [ ] Implement a per-tenant burst detector that can temporarily cap burst amplification (short-term rate-limit policy). (Owner: SRE-tactics)
- [ ] Add a synthetic KV-cache sanity test: simulate node churn and measure token-latency impact; add to release checklist. (Owner: infra-applied-ml)
- [ ] Update runbook: explicit step to check autoscaler audit log + recent merges before manual scale decisions. (Owner: Jordan)

Runbook excerpt (quick actionable steps for oncall):
1) When p95 increases and rejected_requests spike: check autoscaler audit log for recent merges in last 60 minutes (ops-configs).
   - If found, open a config-issue and consider quick rollback to last stable commit.
2) If scale events occurred rapidly (>=3 within 15m): consider manual stabilization — either pause autoscaler or set min_replicas to current capacity for 10m.
3) If KV-cache eviction spike is present: avoid rolling restarts; prefer manual scale + warmup or reduce new node join rate.
4) Identify noisy tenant: run rejected_requests_by_tenant; if a single tenant is >30% of rejections, apply temporary ingress rate-limit and notify Solutions Eng.
5) After mitigation, monitor for 45m before closing incident; capture implicated commits and open postmortem ticket.

Unresolved questions / followups we need to answer in postmortem:
- Should autoscaler parameters be different for dedicated pools with heavy KV-cache state? Maybe a separate policy class.
- Can we improve LB/application readiness signals so readiness aligns with KV cache warm state?
- What are safe defaults for growth_factor/hysteresis to balance fast reaction vs oscillation for our workload?

Notes for the postmortem doc (to be expanded):
- Include timeline with precise metric graphs (cpu, p95, eviction rate).
- Surface the ops-configs merge + author + PR review notes.
- Quantify customer impact: number of requests rejected, affected tenants, SLA deltas.
- Proposed remediation plan and rollout gating timeline.

Slack references / useful links:
- #sre-dedicated thread: https://slack.redwood.ai/archives/C0ABCDEF-incident-4521 (link to conversation)
- Ops PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/ops-configs/pull/128
- Dashboard: grafana/redwood/dedicated-pool-7

Final quick takeaways (TL;DR):
- Root cause: ops-configs autoscaler parameter change reduced hysteresis and increased growth_factor; combined with a short noisy-tenant burst, it triggered repeated scale events. Rapid node churn amplified KV-cache eviction and transiently raised p95 and rejections.
- Short-term fix: revert params, manual scale to stabilize, isolate noisy tenant.
- Long-term: introduce gated canary for autoscaler changes, per-pool class adjustments, synthetic cache-warm tests, and config-change correlation alerts.

---
Notes to daytime owner: ping me (Jordan) in #sre-dedicated if you want the raw metric queries or the temporary ingress rule details. This doc is intentionally lightweight — will expand into full postmortem and attach metric screenshots during business hours.
